claim: Nearly 1 billion people experience severe food insecurity.
source: Undernutrition remains a major global health crisis, with nearly 1 billion people experiencing severe food insecurity.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a factual statistic about global food insecurity.

claim: Infectious disease is the leading cause of morbidity and mortality for malnourished individuals.
source: Malnourished individuals are especially vulnerable to infectious diseases, which is the leading cause of morbidity and mortality for this population.
evidence: This claim is supported by established knowledge in the field and is presented as a known fact.

claim: Malnourished mice show an inability to control sublethal Listeria monocytogenes infection.
source: Malnourished mice show an inability to control sublethal Listeria monocytogenes infection, reduced immune cell function and expansion, and early contraction before pathogen clearance.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the experimental work presented in the manuscript, supported by data in Figure 2.

claim: Malnourished mice exhibit reduced immune cell function and expansion.
source: Malnourished mice show an inability to control sublethal Listeria monocytogenes infection, reduced immune cell function and expansion, and early contraction before pathogen clearance.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data throughout the manuscript, including Figures 2, 3, and 4.

claim: Malnourished mice show early immune cell contraction before pathogen clearance.
source: Malnourished mice show an inability to control sublethal Listeria monocytogenes infection, reduced immune cell function and expansion, and early contraction before pathogen clearance.
evidence: This finding is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 2 and 3.

claim: Myelopoiesis is particularly affected by malnutrition, with fewer neutrophils and monocytes present both before and after infection.
source: Myelopoiesis is particularly affected, with fewer neutrophils and monocytes present both before and after infection in malnourished mice.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data in Figure 4.

claim: Refeeding restores body mass in malnourished mice.
source: While refeeding restores body mass, lymphoid organ cellularity, and T cell responses, refed mice remain susceptible to Listeria infection, revealing that recovery from lymphoid atrophy alone is not sufficient to restore protective immunity.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5.

claim: Refeeding restores lymphoid organ cellularity in malnourished mice.
source: While refeeding restores body mass, lymphoid organ cellularity, and T cell responses, refed mice remain susceptible to Listeria infection, revealing that recovery from lymphoid atrophy alone is not sufficient to restore protective immunity.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5.

claim: Refeeding restores T cell responses in malnourished mice.
source: While refeeding restores body mass, lymphoid organ cellularity, and T cell responses, refed mice remain susceptible to Listeria infection, revealing that recovery from lymphoid atrophy alone is not sufficient to restore protective immunity.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6.

claim: Refed mice remain susceptible to Listeria infection despite recovery of body mass and lymphoid cellularity.
source: While refeeding restores body mass, lymphoid organ cellularity, and T cell responses, refed mice remain susceptible to Listeria infection, revealing that recovery from lymphoid atrophy alone is not sufficient to restore protective immunity.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data in Figure 6.

claim: Recovery from lymphoid atrophy alone is not sufficient to restore protective immunity.
source: While refeeding restores body mass, lymphoid organ cellularity, and T cell responses, refed mice remain susceptible to Listeria infection, revealing that recovery from lymphoid atrophy alone is not sufficient to restore protective immunity.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the experimental findings from the refeeding experiments shown in Figure 6.

claim: Peripheral neutrophils and monocytes fail to fully recover in refed animals.
source: Accordingly, peripheral neutrophils and monocytes fail to fully recover, and emergency myelopoiesis remains impaired in refed animals.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6.

claim: Emergency myelopoiesis remains impaired in refed animals.
source: Accordingly, peripheral neutrophils and monocytes fail to fully recover, and emergency myelopoiesis remains impaired in refed animals.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6.

claim: Dysregulated myelopoiesis is a link between prior nutritional state and immunocompetency.
source: Altogether, this work identifies dysregulated myelopoiesis as a link between prior nutritional state and immunocompetency, indicating that food scarcity is an immunologic risk factor, even after nutritional recovery.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental findings throughout the manuscript.

claim: Food scarcity is an immunologic risk factor, even after nutritional recovery.
source: Altogether, this work identifies dysregulated myelopoiesis as a link between prior nutritional state and immunocompetency, indicating that food scarcity is an immunologic risk factor, even after nutritional recovery.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental findings, particularly the refeeding experiments.

claim: Almost 500 million adults are affected by undernutrition worldwide.
source: Almost 500 million adults and over 200 million children are affected by undernutrition worldwide, with over half of all childhood deaths linked to undernutrition (United Nations, 2021; UNICEF, 1998).
evidence: This statistic is cited from external sources (United Nations, 2021; UNICEF, 1998).

claim: Over 200 million children are affected by undernutrition worldwide.
source: Almost 500 million adults and over 200 million children are affected by undernutrition worldwide, with over half of all childhood deaths linked to undernutrition (United Nations, 2021; UNICEF, 1998).
evidence: This statistic is cited from external sources (United Nations, 2021; UNICEF, 1998).

claim: Over half of all childhood deaths are linked to undernutrition.
source: Almost 500 million adults and over 200 million children are affected by undernutrition worldwide, with over half of all childhood deaths linked to undernutrition (United Nations, 2021; UNICEF, 1998).
evidence: This statistic is cited from external sources (United Nations, 2021; UNICEF, 1998).

claim: Undernutrition numbers worsened in the past 5 years due to economic instability from the COVID-19 pandemic.
source: In the past 5 years, these numbers worsened due to economic instability ushered by COVID-19 pandemic, and they are projected to further increase throughout the impending climate crisis (Mbow et al., 2019; United Nations, 2022).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to external sources (Mbow et al., 2019; United Nations, 2022).

claim: Undernutrition numbers are projected to further increase throughout the impending climate crisis.
source: In the past 5 years, these numbers worsened due to economic instability ushered by COVID-19 pandemic, and they are projected to further increase throughout the impending climate crisis (Mbow et al., 2019; United Nations, 2022).
evidence: This projection is supported by citations to external sources (Mbow et al., 2019; United Nations, 2022).

claim: In patients with undernutrition, the largest contributor to morbidity and mortality is infectious disease.
source: In patients with undernutrition, the largest contributor to morbidity and mortality is infectious disease (Fan et al., 2022; Rice et al., 2000).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to external sources (Fan et al., 2022; Rice et al., 2000).

claim: Undernutrition alone puts patients, especially children, at a higher risk of developing long-lasting disability or dying from an infection.
source: It has been demonstrated that undernutrition alone puts patients, especially children, at a higher risk of developing long-lasting disability or dying from an infection (Antwi, 2011; Bhargava, 2016; Bourke et al., 2016; Caulfield et al., 2004; Rice et al., 2000; Schlaudecker et al., 2011; Sinha et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to external sources.

claim: Chronically undernourished individuals have impaired barrier function.
source: In addition to increased susceptibility to infection, chronically undernourished individuals have been reported to have impaired barrier function, atrophy of immune organs, and less effective responses to vaccines (Bhattacharjee et al., 2021; Bourke et al., 2016; Collins and Belkaid, 2022; Prendergast, 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to external sources.

claim: Chronically undernourished individuals have atrophy of immune organs.
source: In addition to increased susceptibility to infection, chronically undernourished individuals have been reported to have impaired barrier function, atrophy of immune organs, and less effective responses to vaccines (Bhattacharjee et al., 2021; Bourke et al., 2016; Collins and Belkaid, 2022; Prendergast, 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to external sources.

claim: Chronically undernourished individuals have less effective responses to vaccines.
source: In addition to increased susceptibility to infection, chronically undernourished individuals have been reported to have impaired barrier function, atrophy of immune organs, and less effective responses to vaccines (Bhattacharjee et al., 2021; Bourke et al., 2016; Collins and Belkaid, 2022; Prendergast, 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to external sources.

claim: Undernutrition is the leading cause of secondary immunodeficiency in the world.
source: In keeping with this, undernutrition is the leading cause of secondary immunodeficiency in the world (Chinen and Shearer, 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to an external source (Chinen and Shearer, 2010).

claim: The first link between undernutrition and poor infection outcomes was posited over a century ago.
source: Despite the first link between undernutrition and poor infection outcomes being posited over a century ago, the cellular mechanisms underlying undernutrition-induced immunodeficiency remain poorly resolved (Bourke et al., 2019; Bourke et al., 2016; Hess, 1932; Newsholme, 1908).
evidence: This historical claim is supported by citations to early sources (Hess, 1932; Newsholme, 1908).

claim: The cellular mechanisms underlying undernutrition-induced immunodeficiency remain poorly resolved.
source: Despite the first link between undernutrition and poor infection outcomes being posited over a century ago, the cellular mechanisms underlying undernutrition-induced immunodeficiency remain poorly resolved (Bourke et al., 2019; Bourke et al., 2016; Hess, 1932; Newsholme, 1908).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to recent review articles (Bourke et al., 2019; Bourke et al., 2016).

claim: T, B, and NK cells are reduced in the periphery of patients with undernutrition.
source: Patient data and animal studies suggest that T, B, and NK cells are reduced in the periphery of patients with undernutrition and experimental animals (Campbell et al., 2020; Cason et al., 1986; Contreras et al., 2018; Howard et al., 1999; Nájera et al., 2004; Saha et al., 1977; Schattner et al., 1990; Yang et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to patient data and animal studies.

claim: Animal models of short-term fasting and protein deficiency impair T cell expansion.
source: Moreover, animal models of short-term fasting and protein deficiency have been found to impair T cell expansion, cytokine production, and memory recall responses (Chatraw et al., 2008; Iyer et al., 2012; Mengheri et al., 1992; Procaccini et al., 2012; Saucillo et al., 2014; Taylor et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to animal studies.

claim: Animal models of short-term fasting and protein deficiency impair T cell cytokine production.
source: Moreover, animal models of short-term fasting and protein deficiency have been found to impair T cell expansion, cytokine production, and memory recall responses (Chatraw et al., 2008; Iyer et al., 2012; Mengheri et al., 1992; Procaccini et al., 2012; Saucillo et al., 2014; Taylor et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to animal studies.

claim: Animal models of short-term fasting and protein deficiency impair T cell memory recall responses.
source: Moreover, animal models of short-term fasting and protein deficiency have been found to impair T cell expansion, cytokine production, and memory recall responses (Chatraw et al., 2008; Iyer et al., 2012; Mengheri et al., 1992; Procaccini et al., 2012; Saucillo et al., 2014; Taylor et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to animal studies.

claim: The contribution of lymphocyte dysfunction to nutritionally acquired immunodeficiency is well established.
source: While the contribution of lymphocyte dysfunction to nutritionally acquired immunodeficiency is well established, the impact of prolonged undernutrition on other immune cell populations and the role they play in disease susceptibility is not well understood.
evidence: This is presented as established knowledge based on the preceding citations and discussion.

claim: The impact of prolonged undernutrition on other immune cell populations and their role in disease susceptibility is not well understood.
source: While the contribution of lymphocyte dysfunction to nutritionally acquired immunodeficiency is well established, the impact of prolonged undernutrition on other immune cell populations and the role they play in disease susceptibility is not well understood.
evidence: This identifies a knowledge gap that the current study aims to address.

claim: Prior studies have reported disparate impacts of undernutrition on immunity and infection.
source: Prior studies have reported disparate impacts of undernutrition on immunity and infection, with some finding dietary or caloric restriction enhances inflammation or immunity, while others observing a loss in immune function (Bhattacharjee et al., 2021; Campbell et al., 2020; Chatraw et al., 2008; Collins et al., 2019; Han et al., 2023; Hasegawa et al., 2012; Iyer et al., 2012; Palma et al., 2021; Pena-Cruz et al., 1989; Piccio et al., 2008; Starr et al., 2016; Sun et al., 2001; Taylor et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations showing conflicting results in the literature.

claim: Discrepancies in the impact of undernutrition on immunity likely result from whether animals are subjected to caloric restriction alone or if there is also corresponding limitation in key micro- and macronutrients.
source: These discrepancies likely result from whether animals are subjected to caloric restriction alone or if there is also corresponding limitation in key micro- and macronutrients and whether the restriction in food intake is administered as a short-term fast or is sustained (Cerqueira and Kowaltowski, 2010; Contreras et al., 2018; Meydani et al., 2016; Palma et al., 2021; Yan et al., 2021).
evidence: This is an inference based on cited literature that discusses different dietary restriction models.

claim: Caloric and nutrient restriction diets significantly differ in weight loss patterns, physiology, and nutritional state.
source: To this end, caloric and nutrient restriction diets significantly differ in weight loss patterns, physiology, and nutritional state (Cerqueira and Kowaltowski, 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to an external source (Cerqueira and Kowaltowski, 2010).

claim: Both caloric restriction and chronic undernutrition are associated with reduced inflammation.
source: While both diets are associated with reduced inflammation, caloric restriction is understood to support both lifespan and health span, in stark contrast to chronic undernutrition (Collins and Belkaid, 2022; Contreras et al., 2018; Goldberg et al., 2015; Green et al., 2022; Hasegawa et al., 2012; Howard et al., 1999; Jordan et al., 2019; Piccio et al., 2008; Spadaro et al., 2022; Sun et al., 2001; Yang et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to external sources.

claim: Caloric restriction supports both lifespan and health span, in stark contrast to chronic undernutrition.
source: While both diets are associated with reduced inflammation, caloric restriction is understood to support both lifespan and health span, in stark contrast to chronic undernutrition (Collins and Belkaid, 2022; Contreras et al., 2018; Goldberg et al., 2015; Green et al., 2022; Hasegawa et al., 2012; Howard et al., 1999; Jordan et al., 2019; Piccio et al., 2008; Spadaro et al., 2022; Sun et al., 2001; Yang et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to external sources.

claim: There is limited knowledge on whether nutritionally acquired immunodeficiency is reversible.
source: Beyond our mechanistic understanding of nutritionally acquired immunodeficiency, there is limited knowledge on whether this dysfunction is reversible (Contreras et al., 2018; Schattner et al., 1990; Vaisman et al., 2004).
evidence: This identifies a knowledge gap supported by citations to limited prior work.

claim: Current treatment guidelines for patients with undernutrition utilize refeeding protocols that focus on weight gain as the indicator of recovery.
source: Because current treatment guidelines for patients with undernutrition utilize refeeding protocols that focus on weight gain as the indicator of recovery, the effects of refeeding on the immune system are understudied (Ashworth et al., 2003).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to treatment guidelines (Ashworth et al., 2003).

claim: The effects of refeeding on the immune system are understudied.
source: Because current treatment guidelines for patients with undernutrition utilize refeeding protocols that focus on weight gain as the indicator of recovery, the effects of refeeding on the immune system are understudied (Ashworth et al., 2003).
evidence: This identifies a knowledge gap in the field.

claim: Whether prior exposure to malnutrition has durable effects on the ability to control infection following refeeding remains unknown.
source: Moreover, whether prior exposure to malnutrition has durable effects on the ability to control infection following refeeding remains unknown.
evidence: This identifies a specific knowledge gap that the current study addresses.

claim: The 40RD model effectively recapitulates the hallmarks of human undernutrition.
source: We employ a chronic murine dietary restriction model and demonstrate that it effectively recapitulates the hallmarks of human undernutrition.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data in Figure 1.

claim: Chronic undernutrition results in a specific atrophy of immune organs that is not mirrored in essential organs, such as the liver and kidney.
source: We find that chronic undernutrition results in a specific atrophy of immune organs that is not mirrored in essential organs, such as the liver and kidney.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data in Figure 1f.

claim: Loss of lymphoid tissue in undernourished mice is accompanied by a broad reduction in both innate and adaptive immune cell compartments.
source: This loss of lymphoid tissue is accompanied by a broad reduction in both innate and adaptive immune cell compartments.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data in Figures 1, 2, and 4.

claim: Undernourished mice fail to control sublethal L. monocytogenes infection, either succumbing to disease or failing to clear the pathogen long term.
source: Undernourished mice fail to control sublethal L. monocytogenes infection, either succumbing to disease or failing to clear the pathogen long term.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data in Figure 2.

claim: Undernourished mice undergo the initial phase of immune cell expansion following infection but fail to sustain it, and the response rapidly undergoes contraction.
source: We find that while these mice undergo the initial phase of immune cell expansion following infection, they fail to sustain it, and the response rapidly undergoes contraction.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data in Figures 2 and 3.

claim: T cells in undernourished mice display muted expansion, accelerated contraction, and impaired effector function.
source: Accordingly, we observe that T cells in these mice display muted expansion, accelerated contraction, and impaired effector function.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data in Figure 3.

claim: Undernutrition selectively impairs steady-state and emergency myelopoiesis.
source: We further find that undernutrition selectively impairs steady-state and emergency myelopoiesis, resulting in reduced neutrophil and monocyte abundance prior to and post-infection.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data in Figure 4.

claim: Undernutrition results in reduced neutrophil and monocyte abundance prior to and post-infection.
source: We further find that undernutrition selectively impairs steady-state and emergency myelopoiesis, resulting in reduced neutrophil and monocyte abundance prior to and post-infection.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data in Figure 4.

claim: Refeeding protocols are sufficient to restore body mass, growth, and reverse global lymphoid atrophy.
source: Finally, we demonstrate that while refeeding protocols are sufficient to restore body mass, growth, and reverse global lymphoid atrophy, refed mice remain more susceptible to infection even months after recovering size and peripheral immune cell numbers.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data in Figures 5 and 6.

claim: Refed mice remain more susceptible to infection even months after recovering size and peripheral immune cell numbers.
source: Finally, we demonstrate that while refeeding protocols are sufficient to restore body mass, growth, and reverse global lymphoid atrophy, refed mice remain more susceptible to infection even months after recovering size and peripheral immune cell numbers.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data in Figure 6.

claim: Refed mice display impaired emergency myelopoiesis as well as neutrophil and monocyte abundance.
source: In contrast to the ability of refeeding to reverse the effects of undernutrition on lymphoid numbers, we go on to show refed mice display impaired emergency myelopoiesis as well as neutrophil and monocyte abundance.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data in Figure 6.

claim: Dysregulated myelopoiesis is a major factor contributing to increased susceptibility to infection during chronic undernutrition.
source: Altogether, our work identifies dysregulated myelopoiesis as a major factor contributing to increased susceptibility to infection during chronic undernutrition.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental findings throughout the manuscript.

claim: Refeeding protocols are not sufficient to reverse defects in the ability of mice to control infection despite outwardly displaying a recovery from malnutrition.
source: Furthermore, we for the first time demonstrate that refeeding protocols are not sufficient to reverse defects in the ability of mice to control infection or dysregulated myelopoiesis, despite outwardly displaying a recovery from malnutrition.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data in Figure 6.

claim: Refeeding protocols are not sufficient to reverse dysregulated myelopoiesis despite outwardly displaying a recovery from malnutrition.
source: Furthermore, we for the first time demonstrate that refeeding protocols are not sufficient to reverse defects in the ability of mice to control infection or dysregulated myelopoiesis, despite outwardly displaying a recovery from malnutrition.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data in Figure 6.

claim: In patients, undernutrition is associated with a consistent weight loss of 10% or more compared to the age-appropriate body weight that occurs in under 6 months and persists for months to years.
source: In patients, undernutrition is associated with (1) a consistent weight loss of 10% or more compared to the age-appropriate body weight that occurs in under 6 months and persists for months to years; (2) stunting of growth; and (3) a change in body composition associated with weight loss (Institute of Medicine, 2000; Maleta, 2006; Martins et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to external sources defining clinical undernutrition.

claim: In patients, undernutrition is associated with stunting of growth.
source: In patients, undernutrition is associated with (1) a consistent weight loss of 10% or more compared to the age-appropriate body weight that occurs in under 6 months and persists for months to years; (2) stunting of growth; and (3) a change in body composition associated with weight loss (Institute of Medicine, 2000; Maleta, 2006; Martins et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to external sources defining clinical undernutrition.

claim: In patients, undernutrition is associated with a change in body composition associated with weight loss.
source: In patients, undernutrition is associated with (1) a consistent weight loss of 10% or more compared to the age-appropriate body weight that occurs in under 6 months and persists for months to years; (2) stunting of growth; and (3) a change in body composition associated with weight loss (Institute of Medicine, 2000; Maleta, 2006; Martins et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to external sources defining clinical undernutrition.

claim: 40RD mice consistently lost 10% of their initial body weight in 4 weeks.
source: Highlighting the ability of the model to reliably generate a state of moderate undernutrition, 40RD mice consistently lost 10% of their initial body weight (IBW) in 4 weeks (Figure 1b) and achieved an average 20% loss of IBW relative to the AL group (Figure 1c).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1b.

claim: 40RD mice achieved an average 20% loss of initial body weight relative to the AL group.
source: Highlighting the ability of the model to reliably generate a state of moderate undernutrition, 40RD mice consistently lost 10% of their initial body weight (IBW) in 4 weeks (Figure 1b) and achieved an average 20% loss of IBW relative to the AL group (Figure 1c).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1c.

claim: Body condition scores decreased significantly in 40RD mice compared to the AL group over the course of 4 weeks.
source: At the same time, BCSs decreased significantly in 40RD mice compared to the AL group over the course of 4 weeks (Figure 1d).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1d.

claim: The decrease in weight and conditioning in 40RD mice was accompanied by delayed growth and stunting, as measured by body length.
source: This decrease in weight and conditioning was further accompanied by delayed growth and stunting in 40RD mice, as measured by body length (Figure 1e).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1e.

claim: Patients with undernutrition exhibit severe lymphoid organ atrophy.
source: Beyond these gross changes in body condition, patients with undernutrition also exhibit severe lymphoid organ atrophy (Beisel, 1996; Bourke et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to external sources (Beisel, 1996; Bourke et al., 2016).

claim: 40RD mice exhibited a reduction in spleen, thymus, and lymph node size and mass, while organs such as the liver and kidney were unchanged.
source: In keeping with this, we observed a reduction in spleen, thymus, and lymph node size and mass in mice given the 40RD diet, while organs such as the liver and kidney were unchanged, suggesting a specific effect of malnutrition on the immune system (Figure 1f).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1f.

claim: The reduction in lymphoid organ mass in 40RD mice suggests a specific effect of malnutrition on the immune system.
source: In keeping with this, we observed a reduction in spleen, thymus, and lymph node size and mass in mice given the 40RD diet, while organs such as the liver and kidney were unchanged, suggesting a specific effect of malnutrition on the immune system (Figure 1f).
evidence: This is an interpretation of the experimental findings shown in Figure 1f.

claim: 40RD mice exhibited a corresponding reduction in the cellularity of the spleen and thymus.
source: We observed a corresponding reduction in the cellularity of the spleen and thymus, with a more modest loss of cellularity observed in the bone marrow (Figure 1g).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1g.

claim: 40RD mice exhibited a more modest loss of cellularity in the bone marrow compared to spleen and thymus.
source: We observed a corresponding reduction in the cellularity of the spleen and thymus, with a more modest loss of cellularity observed in the bone marrow (Figure 1g).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1g.

claim: The 40RD model reproduces the lymphoid atrophy found in chronically ill patients with undernutrition.
source: Collectively, our findings demonstrate that the 40RD model reproduces the lymphoid atrophy found in chronically ill patients with undernutrition as well as other models of undernutrition in rodents (Beisel, 1996; Bourke et al., 2016; Cason et al., 1986; Contreras et al., 2018; Yang et al., 2009).
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental findings in Figure 1, supported by citations to prior work.

claim: The link between poor infection outcomes and undernutrition has been extensively documented.
source: While the link between poor infection outcomes and undernutrition has been extensively documented, the immunologic mechanisms resulting in poor infection resolution remain unknown (Bourke et al., 2016; Bourke et al., 2019; Dubos, 1955; Ishikawa et al., 2012; Rice et al., 2000).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to external sources.

claim: The immunologic mechanisms resulting in poor infection resolution in undernourished individuals remain unknown.
source: While the link between poor infection outcomes and undernutrition has been extensively documented, the immunologic mechanisms resulting in poor infection resolution remain unknown (Bourke et al., 2016; Bourke et al., 2019; Dubos, 1955; Ishikawa et al., 2012; Rice et al., 2000).
evidence: This identifies a knowledge gap in the field.

claim: All mice in the AL group survived Lm-Ova infection, while nearly half of the 40RD mice became moribund and required euthanasia.
source: Whereas all mice in the AL group survived, nearly half of the 40RD mice became moribund and required euthanasia (Figure 2b).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2b.

claim: 40RD mice displayed higher clinical scores than the AL group throughout the course of infection.
source: Even among surviving mice, the 40RD group displayed higher clinical scores than the AL group throughout the course of infection (Figure 2c).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2c.

claim: 40RD mice failed to clear bacteria at the rate of the AL group, with some mice exhibiting persistent infection.
source: Consistent with this, 40RD mice failed to clear bacteria at the rate of the AL group, with some mice exhibiting persistent infection (Figure 2d).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2d.

claim: Among the AL group, 48.6% and 86.7% of the mice were able to clear bacteria by day 5 and 8 post-infection, respectively, with all mice resolving infection by day 14.
source: Among the AL group, 48.6% and 86.7% of the mice were able to clear bacteria by day 5 and 8 post-infection, respectively, with all mice resolving infection by day 14.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2d.

claim: 40RD mice exhibited delayed clearance kinetics, with only a third of the mice becoming pathogen-free by day 14.
source: In contrast, 40RD mice exhibited delayed clearance kinetics, with only a third of the mice becoming pathogen-free by day 14 (Figure 2d).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2d.

claim: Splenocyte numbers increased at early time points following infection in 40RD mice, but the magnitude and duration of this expansion were significantly lower compared to AL controls.
source: We found that while splenocyte numbers increased at early time points following infection in 40RD mice, the magnitude and duration of this expansion were significantly lower compared to AL controls (Figure 2e).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2e.

claim: Chronic malnutrition is sufficient to induce immune atrophy and abrogate the capacity of mice to mount and sustain an immune response to infection.
source: Thus, chronic malnutrition is sufficient to not only induce immune atrophy but further abrogates the capacity of mice to mount and sustain an immune response to infection.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental findings in Figure 2.

claim: Malnourished patients are known to exhibit a reduction in lymphocyte numbers.
source: As malnourished patients are known to exhibit a reduction in lymphocyte numbers, we assessed whether 40RD mice exhibited signs of lymphopenia following infection (Cason et al., 1986; Nájera et al., 2004; Saha et al., 1977).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to external sources.

claim: Both prior to and after infection, 40RD mice displayed reduced numbers of B cells, CD4 T cells, and CD8 T cells compared to controls.
source: We observed that both prior to and after infection, 40RD mice displayed reduced numbers of B cells, CD4 T cells, and CD8 T cells compared to controls (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: Despite the overall loss in lymphocyte number in 40RD mice, the relative frequency of each population was either unchanged or elevated.
source: Despite this overall loss in lymphocyte number, the relative frequency of each population was either unchanged or elevated, indicating that while malnutrition leads to a global reduction in immune cell numbers, lymphocytes are less impacted than other immune cell populations (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: While malnutrition leads to a global reduction in immune cell numbers, lymphocytes are less impacted than other immune cell populations.
source: Despite this overall loss in lymphocyte number, the relative frequency of each population was either unchanged or elevated, indicating that while malnutrition leads to a global reduction in immune cell numbers, lymphocytes are less impacted than other immune cell populations (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is an interpretation of the experimental findings shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: CD8 T cells play a role in resolving intracellular bacterial infections.
source: Considering the role CD8 T cells play in resolving intracellular bacterial infections and the failure of 40RD mice to clear infection at later time points, we next examined whether the kinetics of T cell expansion and contraction were similarly impacted.
evidence: This is established knowledge in immunology.

claim: The antigen-experienced and short-lived effector CD8+ T cell numbers were significantly reduced throughout the infection in 40RD mice.
source: We found that the antigen-experienced (CD44+) and short-lived effector (CD127lowKLRG1high) CD8+ T cell numbers were significantly reduced throughout the infection (Figure 3a, b).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3a, b.

claim: Effector-like CD8+ T cell populations in 40RD mice expanded minimally during early and peak response and contracted quickly by day 14, prior to pathogen clearance.
source: These effector-like populations expanded minimally during early and peak response and contracted quickly by day 14, prior to pathogen clearance in 40RD mice.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3a, b.

claim: T cells from undernourished mice displayed both a decreased frequency of cytokine-producing cells and a decreased capacity for producing cytokines on a per-cell basis.
source: We observed that T cells from undernourished mice displayed both a decreased frequency of cytokine-producing cells and a decreased capacity for producing cytokines on a per-cell basis (Figure 3c–e).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3c–e.

claim: Impaired T cell function along with insufficient T cell expansion and premature contraction prior to pathogen clearance contribute to the failure of chronically undernourished mice in controlling L. monocytogenes infection.
source: Altogether, these findings suggest that impaired T cell function along with insufficient T cell expansion and premature contraction prior to pathogen clearance contribute to the failure of chronically undernourished mice in controlling L. monocytogenes infection.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental findings in Figure 3.

claim: Steady-state neutrophil and monocyte levels were significantly lower in undernourished mice, both in absolute numbers and relative abundance.
source: While total bone marrow cellularity was equivalent between the 40RD and AL groups, examination of specific innate immune populations in bone marrow revealed that steady-state neutrophil and monocyte levels were significantly lower in undernourished mice, both in absolute numbers and relative abundance (Figures 1g and 4a–d; Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data shown in Figures 1g, 4a–d, and Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: Splenic neutrophil and monocyte abundance were significantly lower in 40RD mice at steady state and underwent impaired expansion following infection.
source: In keeping with this, we observed that splenic neutrophil and monocyte abundance were significantly lower in 40RD mice at steady state and underwent impaired expansion following infection, with splenic monocyte frequency elevated at steady state and comparable to control mice post-infection (Figure 4b–d; Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4b–d and Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: Total peripheral blood cellularity and neutrophil abundance were significantly reduced by 1 week post-dietary restriction.
source: These steady-state changes could be observed early after mice were placed on the 40RD diet, with total peripheral blood cellularity and neutrophil abundance significantly reduced by 1 week post-dietary restriction (Figure 4—figure supplement 1e, f).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1e, f.

claim: Neutrophil and monocyte production is maintained in the bone marrow during steady-state and through emergency myelopoiesis in both bone marrow and spleen upon infection.
source: Neutrophil and monocyte production is maintained in the bone marrow during steady-state and through emergency myelopoiesis in both bone marrow and spleen upon infection (Janssen et al., 2016; Kim, 2010; Manz and Boettcher, 2014; Yvan-Charvet and Ng, 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to external sources.

claim: Myelopoiesis was significantly impaired in undernourished mice.
source: Consistent with a loss of mature neutrophils and monocytes, we found that myelopoiesis was significantly impaired in undernourished mice.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4.

claim: Pre-GM and GMP cells were present at lower numbers in steady-state 40RD mice within the bone marrow.
source: Within the bone marrow, pre-GM and GMP cells were present at lower numbers in steady-state 40RD mice (Figure 4f, g).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4f, g.

claim: Upon infection, bone marrow progenitor populations in 40RD mice were capable of undergoing expansion, with pre-GM cells failing to reach AL levels, whereas GMP cells reached comparable numbers.
source: Upon infection, these bone marrow progenitor populations were capable of undergoing expansion, with pre-GM cells failing to reach AL levels, whereas GMP cells reached comparable numbers (Figure 4f–h).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4f–h.

claim: 40RD mice displayed diminished numbers and frequency of pre-GM and GMP cells in the spleen both pre- and post-infection.
source: These defects were more exaggerated in the spleen, where 40RD mice displayed diminished numbers and frequency of pre-GM and GMP cells both pre- and post-infection (Figure 4f–h).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4f–h.

claim: Undernutrition impairs steady-state myelopoiesis and extramedullary emergency myelopoiesis, blunting the innate immune response against a bacterial pathogen.
source: Altogether, we find that undernutrition impairs steady-state myelopoiesis and extramedullary emergency myelopoiesis, blunting the innate immune response against a bacterial pathogen.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental findings in Figure 4.

claim: One of the primary strategies taken to support patients with undernutrition with health complications is to refeed them by slowly increasing caloric intake to levels expected for their age group.
source: One of the primary strategies taken to support patients with undernutrition with health complications, including infections, is to refeed them by slowly increasing caloric intake to levels expected for their age group (Ashworth et al., 2003).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to treatment guidelines (Ashworth et al., 2003).

claim: Despite the widespread employment of refeeding protocols, the effects of this intervention on immune dysfunction are not known.
source: Despite the widespread employment, the effects of this intervention on immune dysfunction are not known.
evidence: This identifies a knowledge gap in the field.

claim: The RF group was able to regain initial body weight during the refeed period and continued to gain weight at an accelerated pace for the first month.
source: The RF group was able to regain IBW during the refeed period and continued to gain weight at an accelerated pace for the first month (Figure 5b).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5b.

claim: After the initial increase in weight, the weight gain pace of RF mice slowed down to the same rate as the AL group.
source: After the initial increase in weight, the weight gain pace of RF mice slowed down to the same rate as the AL group (Figure 5c).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5c.

claim: RF mice were able to recover growth but maintained a modest but significantly shorter body length than AL controls for their age.
source: We further observed that while RF mice were able to recover growth, the mice maintained a modest but significantly shorter body length than AL controls for their age (Figure 5d), in keeping with persistent stunting common in patients with undernutrition (Ashworth et al., 2003).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5d.

claim: Persistent stunting is common in patients with undernutrition.
source: We further observed that while RF mice were able to recover growth, the mice maintained a modest but significantly shorter body length than AL controls for their age (Figure 5d), in keeping with persistent stunting common in patients with undernutrition (Ashworth et al., 2003).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to external source (Ashworth et al., 2003).

claim: Cellularity in the spleen, thymus, and bone marrow were comparable between AL and RF groups.
source: Paralleling recovery in weight, we found that cellularity in the spleen, thymus, and bone marrow were comparable between AL and RF groups (Figure 5e).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5e.

claim: The weight of lymphoid organs has returned to the AL levels in the RF group.
source: Moreover, we observed that the weight of lymphoid organs has returned to the AL levels in the RF group (Figure 5f).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5f.

claim: Refeeding intervention is sufficient to restore global lymphoid atrophy.
source: Together, these findings indicate that refeeding intervention is sufficient to restore global lymphoid atrophy.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental findings in Figure 5.

claim: While refeeding was able to limit morbidity compared to 40RD mice, a portion of RF animals succumbed to infection, whereas all AL mice remained viable.
source: While refeeding was able to limit morbidity compared to 40RD mice, a portion of RF animals succumbed to infection, whereas all AL mice remained viable (Figure 5b).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6b.

claim: Mice with ongoing malnutrition maintained the highest pathogen burdens.
source: Consistent with this, we observed that mice with ongoing malnutrition maintained the highest pathogen burdens and that RF mice were unable to resolve infection with the same kinetics as AL mice, with less than half of RF mice clearing bacteria (Figure 5c).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6c.

claim: RF mice were unable to resolve infection with the same kinetics as AL mice, with less than half of RF mice clearing bacteria.
source: Consistent with this, we observed that mice with ongoing malnutrition maintained the highest pathogen burdens and that RF mice were unable to resolve infection with the same kinetics as AL mice, with less than half of RF mice clearing bacteria (Figure 5c).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6c.

claim: Despite refeeding being sufficient to reverse malnutrition-induced lymphoid atrophy, prior exposure to chronic undernutrition leads to persistent susceptibility to infection.
source: These data indicate that despite refeeding being sufficient to reverse malnutrition-induced lymphoid atrophy, prior exposure to chronic undernutrition leads to persistent susceptibility to infection.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental findings in Figure 6.

claim: Post-infection splenic and bone marrow cellularity were equivalent between RF and AL mice.
source: In keeping with the steady-state recovery observed, post-infection splenic and bone marrow cellularity were equivalent between RF and AL mice (Figure 6d).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6d.

claim: T and B cell numbers were restored in RF mice, and all lymphocyte populations underwent comparable expansion to AL controls after infection.
source: Moreover, we found that T and B cell numbers were restored in RF mice, and all lymphocyte populations underwent comparable expansion to AL controls after infection (Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: There were no differences in the number of antigen-experienced T cells in the spleen nor T cell functional capacity between RF and AL mice.
source: Similarly, we observed no differences in the number of antigen-experienced T cells in the spleen nor T cell functional capacity (Figure 6e–g).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6e–g.

claim: Refeeding permits recovery of lymphocyte number, lymphocyte expansion capacity, and T cell function in response to infection.
source: Thus, refeeding permits recovery of lymphocyte number, lymphocyte expansion capacity, and T cell function in response to infection, suggesting lymphocyte dysfunction is unlikely to be responsible for the persistent susceptibility observed.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental findings in Figure 6.

claim: Lymphocyte dysfunction is unlikely to be responsible for the persistent susceptibility to infection observed in RF mice.
source: Thus, refeeding permits recovery of lymphocyte number, lymphocyte expansion capacity, and T cell function in response to infection, suggesting lymphocyte dysfunction is unlikely to be responsible for the persistent susceptibility observed.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the experimental findings in Figure 6.

claim: RF mice displayed impaired peripheral expansion of neutrophil and monocyte populations after infection, both by frequency and number.
source: In contrast to the restoration of the lymphocyte response, we observed sustained defects in the myeloid compartment. RF mice displayed impaired peripheral expansion of neutrophil and monocyte populations after infection, both by frequency and number, with neutrophil number diminished in steady-state RF mice as well (Figure 6i, j; Figure 6—figure supplement 2a, b).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6i, j and Figure 6—figure supplement 2a, b.

claim: Neutrophil number was diminished in steady-state RF mice.
source: In contrast to the restoration of the lymphocyte response, we observed sustained defects in the myeloid compartment. RF mice displayed impaired peripheral expansion of neutrophil and monocyte populations after infection, both by frequency and number, with neutrophil number diminished in steady-state RF mice as well (Figure 6i, j; Figure 6—figure supplement 2a, b).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6i, j and Figure 6—figure supplement 2a, b.

claim: Within the bone marrow of RF mice, there was a reduced frequency in steady-state monocyte and neutrophil abundance as well as reduced total neutrophil numbers.
source: Within the bone marrow, we observed a reduced frequency in steady-state monocyte and neutrophil abundance as well as reduced total neutrophil numbers; however, both populations expanded upon infection, reaching control numbers (Figure 6—figure supplement 2c–f).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 2c–f.

claim: Both monocyte and neutrophil populations in the bone marrow of RF mice expanded upon infection, reaching control numbers.
source: Within the bone marrow, we observed a reduced frequency in steady-state monocyte and neutrophil abundance as well as reduced total neutrophil numbers; however, both populations expanded upon infection, reaching control numbers (Figure 6—figure supplement 2c–f).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 2c–f.

claim: Myeloid progenitor populations were not perturbed in the bone marrow of RF mice.
source: Whereas myeloid progenitor populations were not perturbed in the bone marrow, we found that RF mice exhibited significantly reduced frequency and numbers of splenic pre-GM and GMP cells following infection, with the GMP population also diminished in steady-state mice (Figure 6j–l; Figure 6—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 3.

claim: RF mice exhibited significantly reduced frequency and numbers of splenic pre-GM and GMP cells following infection.
source: Whereas myeloid progenitor populations were not perturbed in the bone marrow, we found that RF mice exhibited significantly reduced frequency and numbers of splenic pre-GM and GMP cells following infection, with the GMP population also diminished in steady-state mice (Figure 6j–l; Figure 6—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6j–l and Figure 6—figure supplement 3.

claim: The GMP population was also diminished in steady-state RF mice.
source: Whereas myeloid progenitor populations were not perturbed in the bone marrow, we found that RF mice exhibited significantly reduced frequency and numbers of splenic pre-GM and GMP cells following infection, with the GMP population also diminished in steady-state mice (Figure 6j–l; Figure 6—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6j–l and Figure 6—figure supplement 3.

claim: Refeeding intervention uncouples a global recovery in lymphoid atrophy from an enduring impairment in emergency myelopoiesis, resulting in lasting susceptibility to infection.
source: Altogether, our findings demonstrate that refeeding intervention uncouples a global recovery in lymphoid atrophy from an enduring impairment in emergency myelopoiesis, resulting in lasting susceptibility to infection.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental findings in Figure 6.

claim: Sustained malnutrition results in global lymphoid atrophy, with loss of both innate and adaptive immune cell populations.
source: Here, we employ a murine model of chronic undernutrition that phenocopies many of the hallmarks of human undernutrition (stunting, wasting, and changes in body composition) to characterize how chronic malnutrition leads to nutritionally acquired immunodeficiency. We demonstrate that sustained malnutrition results in global lymphoid atrophy, with loss of both innate and adaptive immune cell populations.
evidence: This is a summary of primary findings from the manuscript.

claim: There is a unique and severe impairment in neutrophil abundance and myelopoiesis in malnourished mice, with a similar but more modest effect on monocytes.
source: Additionally, we identified a unique and severe impairment in neutrophil abundance and myelopoiesis, with a similar but more modest effect on monocytes.
evidence: This is a summary of primary findings from the manuscript.

claim: The combination of diminished homeostatic levels of neutrophils and monocytes along with impaired emergency myelopoiesis leads to poor control of early L. monocytogenes infection.
source: Our data suggest that the combination of diminished homeostatic levels of these critical myeloid populations along with impaired emergency myelopoiesis leads to poor control of early L. monocytogenes infection, while a blunted T cell response to infection and their premature contraction results in lack of effective infection resolution.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the experimental findings throughout the manuscript.

claim: A blunted T cell response to infection and their premature contraction results in lack of effective infection resolution in malnourished mice.
source: Our data suggest that the combination of diminished homeostatic levels of these critical myeloid populations along with impaired emergency myelopoiesis leads to poor control of early L. monocytogenes infection, while a blunted T cell response to infection and their premature contraction results in lack of effective infection resolution.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the experimental findings throughout the manuscript.

claim: Restoring food access permitted mice to regain weight and size as well as reverse many signs of immunodeficiency.
source: We then tested whether a refeeding intervention could restore protective immunity to infection. We found that restoring food access permitted mice to regain weight and size as well as reverse many signs of immunodeficiency.
evidence: This is a summary of primary findings from the refeeding experiments.

claim: Refeeding was sufficient to recover lymphoid organ atrophy, the abundance of most circulating lymphocytes, and T cell cytokine production.
source: Refeeding was sufficient to recover lymphoid organ atrophy, the abundance of most circulating lymphocytes, and T cell cytokine production.
evidence: This is a summary of primary findings from the refeeding experiments.

claim: Refed mice continued to display increased susceptibility to L. monocytogenes infection along with sustained defects in neutrophil and monocyte abundance and emergency myelopoiesis.
source: Nonetheless, refed mice continued to display increased susceptibility to L. monocytogenes infection along with sustained defects in neutrophil and monocyte abundance and emergency myelopoiesis.
evidence: This is a summary of primary findings from the refeeding experiments.

claim: Exposure to chronic undernutrition can result in lasting changes to specific compartments of the immune system, with long-term implications for the health of the individual even after recovering growth and size.
source: These data demonstrate that exposure to chronic undernutrition can result in lasting changes to specific compartments of the immune system, with long-term implications for the health of the individual even after recovering growth and size.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental findings throughout the manuscript.

claim: Previous studies have suggested that impaired pathogen responses during undernutrition are driven by lymphocyte loss and functional impairment.
source: Previous studies have suggested that impaired pathogen responses during undernutrition are driven by lymphocyte loss and functional impairment (Beisel, 1996; Beisel, 1982; Institute of Medicine, 2000).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to external sources.

claim: Low levels of circulating lymphocytes have been well documented in patients with undernutrition and various restrictive diet models.
source: Low levels of circulating lymphocytes have been well documented in patients with undernutrition and various restrictive diet models (Campbell et al., 2020; Cason et al., 1986; Contreras et al., 2018; Howard et al., 1999; Saha et al., 1977; Schattner et al., 1990; Yang et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to external sources.

claim: While lymphocyte defects likely contribute to poor resolution of infection, they are not sufficient to explain why previously malnourished mice remain vulnerable to infection.
source: Our data from the refeeding model suggest that while these defects likely contribute to poor resolution of infection, they are not sufficient to explain why previously malnourished mice remain vulnerable to infection, as these mice recover from lymphoid atrophy and display normal T cell responses.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the experimental findings from the refeeding experiments.

claim: Undernourished mice exhibit a steady-state reduction in circulating T cells.
source: Nonetheless, we find consistent with other groups that undernourished mice exhibit a steady-state reduction in circulating T cells.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data and consistent with prior literature.

claim: Upon infection, the T cell compartment in malnourished mice is capable of undergoing expansion, but the magnitude of this response is blunted and quickly contracts prior to pathogen clearance.
source: Upon infection, the T cell compartment is capable of undergoing expansion in malnourished conditions, but the magnitude of this response is blunted and quickly contracts prior to pathogen clearance.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data in Figure 3.

claim: There was reduced abundance of antigen-experienced T cells throughout the infection in malnourished mice.
source: We also found that there was reduced abundance of antigen-experienced T cells throughout the infection.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data in Figure 3.

claim: The intrinsic ability of T cells from malnourished mice to produce inflammatory cytokines was reduced.
source: Additionally, we found that the intrinsic ability of T cells to produce inflammatory cytokines was reduced.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data in Figure 3.

claim: T cells from patients with undernutrition display reduced function.
source: In keeping with work demonstrating that T cells from patients with undernutrition display reduced function, we find that T cells from malnourished mice have impaired cytokine-producing capacity post-infection.
evidence: This claim is supported by reference to prior work on patients with undernutrition.

claim: T cells from malnourished mice have impaired cytokine-producing capacity post-infection.
source: In keeping with work demonstrating that T cells from patients with undernutrition display reduced function, we find that T cells from malnourished mice have impaired cytokine-producing capacity post-infection.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data in Figure 3.

claim: The work supports clinical observations and earlier studies delineating the relationship of undernutrition on lymphoid atrophy and T cell dysfunction.
source: Altogether, our work supports clinical observations and earlier studies delineating the relationship of undernutrition on lymphoid atrophy and T cell dysfunction and has revealed the reversible nature of these defects after refeeding intervention.
evidence: This is a summary statement connecting the current findings to prior work.

claim: The work has revealed the reversible nature of lymphoid atrophy and T cell dysfunction after refeeding intervention.
source: Altogether, our work supports clinical observations and earlier studies delineating the relationship of undernutrition on lymphoid atrophy and T cell dysfunction and has revealed the reversible nature of these defects after refeeding intervention.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the refeeding experiments.

claim: Exposure to chronic periods of malnutrition results in durable defects in the myeloid compartment.
source: In contrast to the recovery found in the adaptive immune cells after refeeding, our work demonstrates that exposure to chronic periods of malnutrition results in durable defects in the myeloid compartment.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the refeeding experiments.

claim: Undernourished mice display impaired myelopoiesis and a loss in abundance in critical peripheral myeloid populations that does not properly recover upon refeeding.
source: We find that undernourished mice display impaired myelopoiesis and a loss in abundance in critical peripheral myeloid populations that does not properly recover upon refeeding.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the refeeding experiments.

claim: Some small cohort studies have shown that circulating neutrophil numbers are reduced in undernourished children.
source: Indeed, some small cohort studies have shown that circulating neutrophil numbers are reduced in undernourished children and that hematopoiesis is impacted in anorexic patients (Kohama et al., 2021; Vaisman et al., 2004).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to external sources (Kohama et al., 2021; Vaisman et al., 2004).

claim: Hematopoiesis is impacted in anorexic patients.
source: Indeed, some small cohort studies have shown that circulating neutrophil numbers are reduced in undernourished children and that hematopoiesis is impacted in anorexic patients (Kohama et al., 2021; Vaisman et al., 2004).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to external sources (Kohama et al., 2021; Vaisman et al., 2004).

claim: While hematopoiesis and peripheral immune cell numbers are broadly sensitive to an animal's ongoing nutritional status, specific subsets are uniquely sensitive to periods of undernutrition and exhibit nutritional scarring that uncouples their activity from future improvements in dietary intake.
source: Thus, while hematopoiesis and peripheral immune cell numbers are broadly sensitive to an animal's ongoing nutritional status, specific subsets are uniquely sensitive to periods of undernutrition and exhibit nutritional scarring that uncouples their activity from future improvements in dietary intake.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the experimental findings from the refeeding experiments.

claim: Lasting epigenetic changes within the myeloid compartment may occur during exposure to undernutrition, akin to what has been observed for trained immunity.
source: These findings raise the possibility that lasting epigenetic changes within the myeloid compartment occur during exposure to undernutrition, akin to what has been observed for trained immunity (Netea et al., 2020).
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the findings, supported by a citation to work on trained immunity (Netea et al., 2020).

claim: A recent study in a small cohort of undernourished children reported changes in H3 acetylation in peripheral blood mononuclear cells.
source: Indeed, a recent study in a small cohort of undernourished children reported changes in H3 acetylation in peripheral blood mononuclear cells (Kupkova et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to an external source (Kupkova et al., 2021).

claim: The extent to which the findings apply more broadly to other models of bacterial infection or innate inflammation is unclear.
source: While this work provides a novel link between myelopoiesis and nutritional state, many questions remain. Our study investigated the effect of chronic undernutrition during L. monocytogenes infection; however, the extent to which these findings apply more broadly to other models of bacterial infection or innate inflammation is unclear.
evidence: This acknowledges a limitation of the current study.

claim: The malnutrition model broadly restricted food intake without regard to the components of diet that are required for immunocompetency.
source: Moreover, our malnutrition model broadly restricted food intake without regard to the components of diet that are required for immunocompetency nor consideration for potential interactions of the magnitude of food restriction with immunodeficiency and the rate of onset.
evidence: This describes a limitation of the experimental design.

claim: The study focused on the effects of dietary restriction on adult, normal weight mice.
source: In addition, our study focused on the effects of dietary restriction on adult, normal weight mice.
evidence: This describes a limitation of the experimental design.

claim: Whether similar phenotypes would emerge if obese animals were dietarily restricted is not clear.
source: Whether similar phenotypes would emerge if obese animals were dietarily restricted and if weight loss was achieved through pharmacologic means (e.g. GLP-1 targeted drugs) is not clear.
evidence: This acknowledges a limitation and area for future investigation.

claim: How similar dietary restriction might affect the immune system if it were initiated in juvenile mice is not addressed.
source: Likewise, how similar dietary restriction might affect the immune system if it were initiated in juvenile mice is not addressed here.
evidence: This acknowledges a limitation and area for future investigation.

claim: Additional work is needed to address whether the changes in myelopoiesis are due to changes within the hematopoietic compartment, non-hematopoietic cells, and/or to systemic levels of key cytokines and hormones.
source: Mechanistically, additional work is needed to address whether the changes in myelopoiesis are due to changes within the hematopoietic compartment, non-hematopoietic cells, and/or to systemic levels of key cytokines and hormones – such as G-CSF, interferons, and leptin – both in malnourished and refed mice.
evidence: This identifies areas for future mechanistic investigation.

claim: The known impact dietary restriction has on microbiota composition and how this might durably impact the immune system is unaccounted for in this work.
source: Finally, the known impact dietary restriction has on microbiota composition and in turn how this might durably impact the immune system is unaccounted for in this work and warrants investigation (Gordon et al., 2012; Blanton et al., 2016).
evidence: This acknowledges a limitation and area for future investigation, supported by citations to external sources (Gordon et al., 2012; Blanton et al., 2016).

claim: The work offers new insight into the contribution of myelopoiesis in nutritionally acquired immunodeficiency and the ability of refeeding intervention to treat these defects.
source: Altogether, our work offers new insight into the contribution of myelopoiesis in nutritionally acquired immunodeficiency and the ability of refeeding intervention to treat these defects.
evidence: This is a summary statement of the contributions of the work.

claim: The burden of morbidity and mortality of infections on undernourished individuals is one of the leading global health crises.
source: The burden of morbidity and mortality of infections on undernourished individuals is one of the leading global health crises, and evidence of impaired vaccine responses in undernourished people is putting in question the world's ability to protect the most vulnerable populations with its most reliable strategies for prevention (Bhattacharjee et al., 2021; Bhargava, 2016; Bourke et al., 2019; Bourke et al., 2016; Dubos, 1955; Ishikawa et al., 2012; Prendergast, 2015; Rice et al., 2000; Saha et al., 1977).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to external sources.

claim: Evidence of impaired vaccine responses in undernourished people is putting in question the world's ability to protect the most vulnerable populations with its most reliable strategies for prevention.
source: The burden of morbidity and mortality of infections on undernourished individuals is one of the leading global health crises, and evidence of impaired vaccine responses in undernourished people is putting in question the world's ability to protect the most vulnerable populations with its most reliable strategies for prevention (Bhattacharjee et al., 2021; Bhargava, 2016; Bourke et al., 2019; Bourke et al., 2016; Dubos, 1955; Ishikawa et al., 2012; Prendergast, 2015; Rice et al., 2000; Saha et al., 1977).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to external sources.

claim: The work provides evidence that even prior exposure to food scarcity may be sufficient to permanently alter future immune responses.
source: We provide evidence that even prior exposure to food scarcity may be sufficient to permanently alter future immune responses.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental findings, particularly the refeeding experiments.

claim: The current dietary status of an individual may be insufficient information to understand the impact nutrition has on their immune system.
source: This suggests that the current dietary status of an individual may be insufficient information to understand the impact nutrition has on their immune system.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the experimental findings showing persistent defects after refeeding.

claim: Future work delineating the specific components of diet required to sustain immune health in the face of food scarcity will be critical for developing nutritional interventions or broader food supplementation programs for at-risk populations.
source: Future work delineating the specific components of diet required to sustain immune health in the face of food scarcity will be critical for developing nutritional interventions or broader food supplementation programs for at-risk populations.
evidence: This is a recommendation for future research based on the findings.

claim: Periods of poverty and food insecurity may be an important factor in patient medical history as well as for formulating global health policy.
source: We believe that this work indicates periods of poverty and food insecurity may be an important factor in patient medical history as well as for formulating global health policy in these areas.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental findings showing persistent defects after refeeding.
